title: Orchestral Suite No. 3 in D major
hook: Trumpets, drums and French dances, and at the centre the Air, for strings alone.

painting.title: La Camargo Dancing
painting.pairingNote: The star dancer of the Paris Opéra around 1730, the years of this suite; the French style of dancing that Bach’s gavottes, bourrée and gigue imitate.

facts: Bach wrote four orchestral suites. He called them *ouvertures*, after their long opening movements, and they were not planned as a set. The oldest source for No. 3 is a set of parts from about 1730 in Leipzig, written out partly by Bach himself and partly by his son Carl Philipp Emanuel and his pupil Johann Ludwig Krebs.

In 1729 Bach took over the Collegium Musicum, a music society founded by Telemann, which gave free concerts at Gottfried Zimmermann’s coffee house in Leipzig, including works for orchestra. A suite like this one may well have been heard there.

A suite of this kind was a German imitation of French court music: a grand [[french-overture|French overture]], then a string of dances. This one is festive, with three trumpets, timpani, two oboes and strings.

The second movement, the Air, is for strings alone. In 1871 the violinist August Wilhelmj arranged it in C major so that the melody could be played entirely on the violin’s lowest string, and it became famous as the “Air on the G String”.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a grand ceremonial opening (I), a slow song for strings (II), and three quick French dances (III–V).

movements.heading: Ouverture
movements.title: Ouverture
movements.summary: A slow, majestic opening in jerky dotted rhythms, with trumpets and drums, played twice. Then the tempo leaps forward: the instruments enter one after another on a busy theme, as in a [[fugue|fugue]], and the first violin steps out for solo passages, as if this were a concerto. At the end the slow, dotted music returns briefly.

mainIdeas.name: The slow music
mainIdeas.description: stately chords with a long-short “dotted” rhythm, like a royal entrance.

mainIdeas.name: The fast theme
mainIdeas.description: a lively run of notes that each part takes up in turn.

stops.hear: Trumpets, drums and full orchestra in grand, jerky, long-short rhythms
stops.happening: The slow opening of a [[french-overture|French overture]]

stops.hear: The same grand opening again
Suddenly fast: a busy theme starts in the strings, and the other parts enter one by one
One violin plays quick, brilliant passages over a lighter accompaniment; the full band answers
stops.happening: Solo episodes, like a concerto inside the overture

stops.hear: The music slows again into the dotted, stately rhythm
stops.happening: The opening style returns to close the movement

notice: Listen for the change of speed at about two and three quarter minutes. The slow, heavy dotted music gives way to something light and quick.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Pinnock and The English Concert recorded the suite in June 1978 on period instruments. In the overture they repeat only the slow opening section, not the fast one, which is why the movement lasts about six minutes. On the Spotify album the suite is tracks 8–12, after Suite No. 2.

movements.heading: Air
movements.title: Air
movements.summary: The trumpets, drums and oboes fall silent. Over a steady bass that walks in even steps, the first violins hold a long, high note and then unwind one of the best-known melodies Bach wrote, while the second violins and violas weave their own lines around it. The Air has two halves, the first six bars long and the second twelve, and each is played twice.

mainIdeas.name: The melody
mainIdeas.description: a long held note that blossoms into slow, winding phrases in the first violins.

mainIdeas.name: The bass
mainIdeas.description: even, walking notes that often leap an octave, keeping the slow music moving.

stops.hear: A single long, high violin note over a walking bass, then a slow, winding melody
stops.happening: The first half of the Air, for strings and [[continuo|continuo]] only

stops.hear: The opening long note again
The melody moves into darker, minor-key harmonies before finding its way home
The second half begins once more

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: The melody comes to rest over the bass’s final steps

notice: Listen to the bass rather than the melody. It never stops walking, and it is what keeps such a slow movement from standing still.

movements.heading: Gavotte I–II
movements.title: Gavotte I–II
movements.summary: Two gavottes, a lively French dance in two beats that starts halfway through the bar. The first, with trumpets and drums, is played; then a second gavotte with a different tune; then the first comes back. Each has two halves, and each half is repeated.

mainIdeas.name: Gavotte I
mainIdeas.description: a bright, bouncing tune for the whole orchestra.

mainIdeas.name: Gavotte II
mainIdeas.description: a second tune of its own, which then gives way to the return of the first.

stops.hear: A bright, bouncy dance tune, with trumpets and drums
A different tune, in the same lively step
The first tune returns

notice: A gavotte starts on the second half of the bar, so each phrase seems to take a small step before it lands. Tap along and feel where the strong beat falls.

movements.heading: Bourrée
movements.title: Bourrée
movements.summary: The shortest movement, just over a minute: a quick, cheerful French dance in two, driven along by the trumpets and drums. It has two halves, each played twice.

mainIdeas.name: The bourrée tune
mainIdeas.description: a brisk, rising phrase that starts just before the beat.

stops.hear: A quick, rising dance tune for the whole orchestra
stops.happening: The first half of the bourrée, then its repeat

stops.hear: The tune moves on to new keys before coming home

stops.label: Last 10 seconds
stops.hear: A firm cadence with the trumpets

notice: Count how quickly the movement is over. The bourrée was a fast, light-footed dance, and Bach keeps it short.

movements.heading: Gigue
movements.title: Gigue
movements.summary: A fast, skipping finale in 6/8, with the trumpets ringing out over the strings and oboes. Like the other dances it has two halves, each repeated, and it ends the suite in festive mood.

mainIdeas.name: The gigue tune
mainIdeas.description: a bouncing figure in groups of three, tossed between the orchestra’s sections.

stops.hear: A quick, bouncing tune in groups of three, with the trumpets on top
The same music again
The tune heads into new keys before turning for home
The second half once more

stops.label: Last 15 seconds
stops.hear: Trumpets and drums lead the closing bars

notice: Compare the Gigue’s lilting rhythm in threes with the Bourrée’s brisk two-step just before it.

threads.title: Ceremony and song
threads.body: The trumpets and drums give the outer movements their sense of occasion. The Air, where they are silent, is the still centre of the suite.

threads.title: French manners, German hands
threads.body: The overture and the dances are French forms, the music of Louis XIV’s court. Bach takes them over and fills them with his own [[counterpoint|counterpoint]], several lines moving at once.

threads.title: A second life
threads.body: Wilhelmj’s 1871 arrangement turned the Air into a concert favourite on its own, and it has been arranged and borrowed ever since, as far as pop music: the 1967 song “A Whiter Shade of Pale” used a bar or two of it as a starting point.
